existing_common_goal_anchors.label: def:p08-tense-until-since
existing_common_goal_anchors.title: Kamp's strict U and S operators
existing_common_goal_anchors.declaration_text:
Let \((T,<,V)\) be a linearly ordered temporal structure.  The strict binary
future and past constructors have the clauses
\[
\begin{aligned}
 t\entails U\,A\,B
 &\text{ iff }
 \exists u>t\,[u\entails A\land
   \forall v\,(t<v<u\to v\entails B)],\\
 t\entails S\,A\,B
 &\text{ iff }
 \exists u<t\,[u\entails A\land
   \forall v\,(u<v<t\to v\entails B)].
\end{aligned}
\]
The prefix symbols \(U\) and \(S\) are Kamp's binary future and past formula
constructors, respectively.  Their first operand holds at the witness and
their second operand at every intervening point; they are not metalinguistic
English tense.  They
are needed because Prior's unary future/past operators cannot express all
one-variable first-order order properties.  Their strict witnesses and two
directions distinguish them from the non-strict discrete LTL until fixed in
Section~\ref{sec:modal-temporal-epistemic-02}; the following theorem uses them
\cite{Prior1967,Kamp1968}.

existing_common_goal_anchors.label: thm:p08-kamp
existing_common_goal_anchors.title: Kamp expressive completeness with its order hypothesis
existing_common_goal_anchors.declaration_text:
Kamp's compositional map sends every formula using negation, conjunction, and
his strict \(U,S\) to an equivalent one-free-variable formula in the displayed
first-order language with \(<\) and unary predicates; its truth induction is
valid over every binary structure.  Conversely, over Kamp's class
\(\mathsf{Com}\) of strict linear orders, every uniformly
first-order-definable tense is expressible by such a temporal formula.
\(\mathsf{Com}\) requires greatest lower and least upper bounds for every
nonempty bounded set; it permits discrete orders and endpoints and does not
mean deductive completeness.  The reverse translation is primitive recursive,
but the thesis gives no complexity or output-size bound.  It is not asserted
over all linear orders; Kamp's rational-order Theorem~IV.5 supplies a
counterexample to this four-operation basis.  The full source presentation is
Section~\ref{sec:p09-presentation-n-c-012}.

existing_common_goal_anchors.label: def:p08-ockhamist-peircean
existing_common_goal_anchors.title: Ockhamist and Peircean branching-time evaluation
existing_common_goal_anchors.declaration_text:
On a branching order, a \emph{history} is a maximal linearly ordered set of
moments.  Ockhamist future-tense truth is evaluated at a moment--history pair,
so it can depend on the current history through that moment.  Peircean
future-tense truth is evaluated at a moment and quantifies over branching
futures.  These are semantic evaluation policies, not competing names for CTL
path quantifiers.  Their different evaluation points prevent ambiguity, and
the distinction is used to delimit the computational cards above from this
philosophical survey \cite{Burgess1984}.

existing_common_goal_anchors.label: def:p08-tense-until-since
existing_common_goal_anchors.title: Kamp's strict U and S operators
existing_common_goal_anchors.declaration_text:
Let \((T,<,V)\) be a linearly ordered temporal structure.  The strict binary
future and past constructors have the clauses
\[
\begin{aligned}
 t\entails U\,A\,B
 &\text{ iff }
 \exists u>t\,[u\entails A\land
   \forall v\,(t<v<u\to v\entails B)],\\
 t\entails S\,A\,B
 &\text{ iff }
 \exists u<t\,[u\entails A\land
   \forall v\,(u<v<t\to v\entails B)].
\end{aligned}
\]
The prefix symbols \(U\) and \(S\) are Kamp's binary future and past formula
constructors, respectively.  Their first operand holds at the witness and
their second operand at every intervening point; they are not metalinguistic
English tense.  They
are needed because Prior's unary future/past operators cannot express all
one-variable first-order order properties.  Their strict witnesses and two
directions distinguish them from the non-strict discrete LTL until fixed in
Section~\ref{sec:modal-temporal-epistemic-02}; the following theorem uses them
\cite{Prior1967,Kamp1968}.

existing_common_goal_anchors.label: thm:p08-kamp
existing_common_goal_anchors.title: Kamp expressive completeness with its order hypothesis
existing_common_goal_anchors.declaration_text:
Kamp's compositional map sends every formula using negation, conjunction, and
his strict \(U,S\) to an equivalent one-free-variable formula in the displayed
first-order language with \(<\) and unary predicates; its truth induction is
valid over every binary structure.  Conversely, over Kamp's class
\(\mathsf{Com}\) of strict linear orders, every uniformly
first-order-definable tense is expressible by such a temporal formula.
\(\mathsf{Com}\) requires greatest lower and least upper bounds for every
nonempty bounded set; it permits discrete orders and endpoints and does not
mean deductive completeness.  The reverse translation is primitive recursive,
but the thesis gives no complexity or output-size bound.  It is not asserted
over all linear orders; Kamp's rational-order Theorem~IV.5 supplies a
counterexample to this four-operation basis.  The full source presentation is
Section~\ref{sec:p09-presentation-n-c-012}.

existing_common_goal_anchors.label: def:p08-ockhamist-peircean
existing_common_goal_anchors.title: Ockhamist and Peircean branching-time evaluation
existing_common_goal_anchors.declaration_text:
On a branching order, a \emph{history} is a maximal linearly ordered set of
moments.  Ockhamist future-tense truth is evaluated at a moment--history pair,
so it can depend on the current history through that moment.  Peircean
future-tense truth is evaluated at a moment and quantifies over branching
futures.  These are semantic evaluation policies, not competing names for CTL
path quantifiers.  Their different evaluation points prevent ambiguity, and
the distinction is used to delimit the computational cards above from this
philosophical survey \cite{Burgess1984}.

current_declaration_bindings.label: def:p08-tense-until-since
current_declaration_bindings.title: Kamp's strict U and S operators
current_declaration_bindings.declaration_text:
Let \((T,<,V)\) be a linearly ordered temporal structure.  The strict binary
future and past constructors have the clauses
\[
\begin{aligned}
 t\entails U\,A\,B
 &\text{ iff }
 \exists u>t\,[u\entails A\land
   \forall v\,(t<v<u\to v\entails B)],\\
 t\entails S\,A\,B
 &\text{ iff }
 \exists u<t\,[u\entails A\land
   \forall v\,(u<v<t\to v\entails B)].
\end{aligned}
\]
The prefix symbols \(U\) and \(S\) are Kamp's binary future and past formula
constructors, respectively.  Their first operand holds at the witness and
their second operand at every intervening point; they are not metalinguistic
English tense.  They
are needed because Prior's unary future/past operators cannot express all
one-variable first-order order properties.  Their strict witnesses and two
directions distinguish them from the non-strict discrete LTL until fixed in
Section~\ref{sec:modal-temporal-epistemic-02}; the following theorem uses them
\cite{Prior1967,Kamp1968}.

current_declaration_bindings.label: thm:p08-kamp
current_declaration_bindings.title: Kamp expressive completeness with its order hypothesis
current_declaration_bindings.declaration_text:
Kamp's compositional map sends every formula using negation, conjunction, and
his strict \(U,S\) to an equivalent one-free-variable formula in the displayed
first-order language with \(<\) and unary predicates; its truth induction is
valid over every binary structure.  Conversely, over Kamp's class
\(\mathsf{Com}\) of strict linear orders, every uniformly
first-order-definable tense is expressible by such a temporal formula.
\(\mathsf{Com}\) requires greatest lower and least upper bounds for every
nonempty bounded set; it permits discrete orders and endpoints and does not
mean deductive completeness.  The reverse translation is primitive recursive,
but the thesis gives no complexity or output-size bound.  It is not asserted
over all linear orders; Kamp's rational-order Theorem~IV.5 supplies a
counterexample to this four-operation basis.  The full source presentation is
Section~\ref{sec:p09-presentation-n-c-012}.

current_declaration_bindings.label: def:p08-ockhamist-peircean
current_declaration_bindings.title: Ockhamist and Peircean branching-time evaluation
current_declaration_bindings.declaration_text:
On a branching order, a \emph{history} is a maximal linearly ordered set of
moments.  Ockhamist future-tense truth is evaluated at a moment--history pair,
so it can depend on the current history through that moment.  Peircean
future-tense truth is evaluated at a moment and quantifies over branching
futures.  These are semantic evaluation policies, not competing names for CTL
path quantifiers.  Their different evaluation points prevent ambiguity, and
the distinction is used to delimit the computational cards above from this
philosophical survey \cite{Burgess1984}.

existing_common_goal_anchors.label: def:p08-hybrid-k
existing_common_goal_anchors.title: Basic hybrid logic \(K({\char64})\)
existing_common_goal_anchors.declaration_text:
Extend modal propositional syntax by a disjoint set of nominals
\(i,j,\ldots\) and satisfaction formulas \(@_iA\). In a Kripke model, each
nominal is true at exactly one world, and
\(M,w\models@_iA\) iff \(M,w_i\models A\), where \(w_i\) is the world named by
\(i\). The name \(K(@)\) is necessary to fix the basic normal modal language
with nominals and satisfaction operators, excluding binders and the global
modality. It stands as a formal language/semantics, differs from ordinary
modal \(K\) by internal world names and jumps, and is used by the labelled
tableau on
\hyperref[sheet:tableaux-hybrid-k]{\texttt{sheet:tableaux-hybrid-k}}
\cite{ArecesTenCate2007}.
\index{hybrid logic}\index{nominal!hybrid logic}\index{satisfaction operator}

existing_common_goal_anchors.label: thm:p08-hybrid-tableau
existing_common_goal_anchors.title: Signed-tableau adequacy for basic \(K({\char64})\)
existing_common_goal_anchors.declaration_text:
For the language and semantics of
Definition~\ref{def:p08-hybrid-k}, the complete signed calculus on
\hyperref[sheet:tableaux-hybrid-k]{\texttt{sheet:tableaux-hybrid-k}} has an
open saturated branch from \(@_iA\), for fresh \(i\), exactly when \(A\) is
satisfiable.  Equivalently, every tableau rooted at \(\neg@_iA\) closes exactly
when \(A\) is valid.  The Boolean, modal, satisfaction, and nominal-identity
rules printed on the sheet are all part of the claim.  Binders and the global
modality are outside this exact language and require additional rules.

current_declaration_bindings.label: def:p08-hybrid-k
current_declaration_bindings.title: Basic hybrid logic \(K({\char64})\)
current_declaration_bindings.declaration_text:
Extend modal propositional syntax by a disjoint set of nominals
\(i,j,\ldots\) and satisfaction formulas \(@_iA\). In a Kripke model, each
nominal is true at exactly one world, and
\(M,w\models@_iA\) iff \(M,w_i\models A\), where \(w_i\) is the world named by
\(i\). The name \(K(@)\) is necessary to fix the basic normal modal language
with nominals and satisfaction operators, excluding binders and the global
modality. It stands as a formal language/semantics, differs from ordinary
modal \(K\) by internal world names and jumps, and is used by the labelled
tableau on
\hyperref[sheet:tableaux-hybrid-k]{\texttt{sheet:tableaux-hybrid-k}}
\cite{ArecesTenCate2007}.
\index{hybrid logic}\index{nominal!hybrid logic}\index{satisfaction operator}

existing_common_goal_anchors.label: def:p08-stalnaker-conditional
existing_common_goal_anchors.title: Selection-function counterfactual
existing_common_goal_anchors.declaration_text:
In a Stalnaker model, a selection function has type
\(f:W\times(\mathcal P(W)\setminus\{\varnothing\})\to W\) and satisfies
\(f(w,X)\in X\).  Put
\[
 M,w\models A>B
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 [A]=\varnothing
 \quad\text{or}\quad
 M,f(w,[A])\models B.
\]
Thus impossible antecedents are vacuously true in this selected presentation;
for nonempty antecedents exactly one world is selected.  Centering is the
additional condition \(w\in X\Rightarrow f(w,X)=w\), not part of selection
alone.  The definition is needed because the
connective \(>\) is not material implication and because uniqueness is stronger
than merely having a set of closest worlds. It stands as a semantic clause,
differs from Lewis's sphere semantics through unique selection, and is used to
test conditional excluded middle \cite{Stalnaker1968}.
\index{counterfactual conditional}\index{selection-function semantics}

existing_common_goal_anchors.label: def:p08-lewis-conditional
existing_common_goal_anchors.title: Lewis sphere counterfactual
existing_common_goal_anchors.declaration_text:
A Lewis model assigns each world \(w\) a nonempty family
\(\mathcal S_w\subseteq\mathcal P(W)\) satisfying:
\begin{enumerate}
  \item \(\mathcal S_w\) is linearly ordered by inclusion;
  \item for every \(\mathcal T\subseteq\mathcal S_w\),
    \(\bigcup\mathcal T\in\mathcal S_w\); and
  \item if \(\varnothing\ne\mathcal T\subseteq\mathcal S_w\) and
    \(\bigcap\mathcal T\ne\varnothing\), then
    \(\bigcap\mathcal T\in\mathcal S_w\).
\end{enumerate}
Write \(U_w=\bigcup\mathcal S_w\).  The variably strict clause is
\[
 M,w\models A\Box\!\!\to B
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 [A]\cap U_w=\varnothing
 \quad\text{or}\quad
 \exists S\in\mathcal S_w
 \bigl(S\cap[A]\ne\varnothing\land S\cap[A]\subseteq[B]\bigr).
\]
This clause does not require a least \(A\)-permitting sphere.  The system is
\emph{weakly centered} when, for every \(w\),
\[
 w\in U_w
 \quad\text{and}\quad
 \forall S\in\mathcal S_w\,
   (S\ne\varnothing\to w\in S),
\]
and \emph{centered} when
\(\{w\}\in\mathcal S_w\) for every \(w\).  Nesting makes centering imply weak
centering.  Lewis's \(\mathsf V\), \(\mathsf{VW}\), and \(\mathsf{VC}\)
use, respectively, arbitrary sphere systems of the displayed kind, weakly
centered systems, and centered systems.  The \emph{limit assumption} is the
further condition that, whenever \([A]\cap U_w\ne\varnothing\),
\[
 \exists S\in\mathcal S_w\,
 \bigl(S\cap[A]\ne\varnothing\ \land\
   \forall T\in\mathcal S_w\,
     (T\cap[A]\ne\varnothing\to S\subseteq T)\bigr).
\]
None of these centering clauses entails the limit assumption.  The sphere
definition is needed because there may be several equally close worlds or no
minimal sphere. It stands as a comparative-similarity semantics, differs from
unique selection, and is used for limit-assumption and centering distinctions
\cite{Lewis1973}.
\index{sphere semantics}\index{limit assumption}

current_declaration_bindings.label: def:p08-stalnaker-conditional
current_declaration_bindings.title: Selection-function counterfactual
current_declaration_bindings.declaration_text:
In a Stalnaker model, a selection function has type
\(f:W\times(\mathcal P(W)\setminus\{\varnothing\})\to W\) and satisfies
\(f(w,X)\in X\).  Put
\[
 M,w\models A>B
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 [A]=\varnothing
 \quad\text{or}\quad
 M,f(w,[A])\models B.
\]
Thus impossible antecedents are vacuously true in this selected presentation;
for nonempty antecedents exactly one world is selected.  Centering is the
additional condition \(w\in X\Rightarrow f(w,X)=w\), not part of selection
alone.  The definition is needed because the
connective \(>\) is not material implication and because uniqueness is stronger
than merely having a set of closest worlds. It stands as a semantic clause,
differs from Lewis's sphere semantics through unique selection, and is used to
test conditional excluded middle \cite{Stalnaker1968}.
\index{counterfactual conditional}\index{selection-function semantics}

current_declaration_bindings.label: def:p08-lewis-conditional
current_declaration_bindings.title: Lewis sphere counterfactual
current_declaration_bindings.declaration_text:
A Lewis model assigns each world \(w\) a nonempty family
\(\mathcal S_w\subseteq\mathcal P(W)\) satisfying:
\begin{enumerate}
  \item \(\mathcal S_w\) is linearly ordered by inclusion;
  \item for every \(\mathcal T\subseteq\mathcal S_w\),
    \(\bigcup\mathcal T\in\mathcal S_w\); and
  \item if \(\varnothing\ne\mathcal T\subseteq\mathcal S_w\) and
    \(\bigcap\mathcal T\ne\varnothing\), then
    \(\bigcap\mathcal T\in\mathcal S_w\).
\end{enumerate}
Write \(U_w=\bigcup\mathcal S_w\).  The variably strict clause is
\[
 M,w\models A\Box\!\!\to B
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 [A]\cap U_w=\varnothing
 \quad\text{or}\quad
 \exists S\in\mathcal S_w
 \bigl(S\cap[A]\ne\varnothing\land S\cap[A]\subseteq[B]\bigr).
\]
This clause does not require a least \(A\)-permitting sphere.  The system is
\emph{weakly centered} when, for every \(w\),
\[
 w\in U_w
 \quad\text{and}\quad
 \forall S\in\mathcal S_w\,
   (S\ne\varnothing\to w\in S),
\]
and \emph{centered} when
\(\{w\}\in\mathcal S_w\) for every \(w\).  Nesting makes centering imply weak
centering.  Lewis's \(\mathsf V\), \(\mathsf{VW}\), and \(\mathsf{VC}\)
use, respectively, arbitrary sphere systems of the displayed kind, weakly
centered systems, and centered systems.  The \emph{limit assumption} is the
further condition that, whenever \([A]\cap U_w\ne\varnothing\),
\[
 \exists S\in\mathcal S_w\,
 \bigl(S\cap[A]\ne\varnothing\ \land\
   \forall T\in\mathcal S_w\,
     (T\cap[A]\ne\varnothing\to S\subseteq T)\bigr).
\]
None of these centering clauses entails the limit assumption.  The sphere
definition is needed because there may be several equally close worlds or no
minimal sphere. It stands as a comparative-similarity semantics, differs from
unique selection, and is used for limit-assumption and centering distinctions
\cite{Lewis1973}.
\index{sphere semantics}\index{limit assumption}

Definition~\ref{def:p08-lewis-conditional}.  The source's limit-free clause is

present_destinations.label: def:p08-stalnaker-conditional
present_destinations.title: Selection-function counterfactual
present_destinations.declaration_text:
In a Stalnaker model, a selection function has type
\(f:W\times(\mathcal P(W)\setminus\{\varnothing\})\to W\) and satisfies
\(f(w,X)\in X\).  Put
\[
 M,w\models A>B
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 [A]=\varnothing
 \quad\text{or}\quad
 M,f(w,[A])\models B.
\]
Thus impossible antecedents are vacuously true in this selected presentation;
for nonempty antecedents exactly one world is selected.  Centering is the
additional condition \(w\in X\Rightarrow f(w,X)=w\), not part of selection
alone.  The definition is needed because the
connective \(>\) is not material implication and because uniqueness is stronger
than merely having a set of closest worlds. It stands as a semantic clause,
differs from Lewis's sphere semantics through unique selection, and is used to
test conditional excluded middle \cite{Stalnaker1968}.
\index{counterfactual conditional}\index{selection-function semantics}

present_destinations.label: def:p08-lewis-conditional
present_destinations.title: Lewis sphere counterfactual
present_destinations.declaration_text:
A Lewis model assigns each world \(w\) a nonempty family
\(\mathcal S_w\subseteq\mathcal P(W)\) satisfying:
\begin{enumerate}
  \item \(\mathcal S_w\) is linearly ordered by inclusion;
  \item for every \(\mathcal T\subseteq\mathcal S_w\),
    \(\bigcup\mathcal T\in\mathcal S_w\); and
  \item if \(\varnothing\ne\mathcal T\subseteq\mathcal S_w\) and
    \(\bigcap\mathcal T\ne\varnothing\), then
    \(\bigcap\mathcal T\in\mathcal S_w\).
\end{enumerate}
Write \(U_w=\bigcup\mathcal S_w\).  The variably strict clause is
\[
 M,w\models A\Box\!\!\to B
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 [A]\cap U_w=\varnothing
 \quad\text{or}\quad
 \exists S\in\mathcal S_w
 \bigl(S\cap[A]\ne\varnothing\land S\cap[A]\subseteq[B]\bigr).
\]
This clause does not require a least \(A\)-permitting sphere.  The system is
\emph{weakly centered} when, for every \(w\),
\[
 w\in U_w
 \quad\text{and}\quad
 \forall S\in\mathcal S_w\,
   (S\ne\varnothing\to w\in S),
\]
and \emph{centered} when
\(\{w\}\in\mathcal S_w\) for every \(w\).  Nesting makes centering imply weak
centering.  Lewis's \(\mathsf V\), \(\mathsf{VW}\), and \(\mathsf{VC}\)
use, respectively, arbitrary sphere systems of the displayed kind, weakly
centered systems, and centered systems.  The \emph{limit assumption} is the
further condition that, whenever \([A]\cap U_w\ne\varnothing\),
\[
 \exists S\in\mathcal S_w\,
 \bigl(S\cap[A]\ne\varnothing\ \land\
   \forall T\in\mathcal S_w\,
     (T\cap[A]\ne\varnothing\to S\subseteq T)\bigr).
\]
None of these centering clauses entails the limit assumption.  The sphere
definition is needed because there may be several equally close worlds or no
minimal sphere. It stands as a comparative-similarity semantics, differs from
unique selection, and is used for limit-assumption and centering distinctions
\cite{Lewis1973}.
\index{sphere semantics}\index{limit assumption}

existing_common_goal_anchors.label: def:p08-adams-conditional
existing_common_goal_anchors.title: Probabilistic assertability of an indicative
existing_common_goal_anchors.declaration_text:
For events with \(P(A)>0\), the Adams-style assertability of ``if \(A\), then
\(B\)'' is governed by \(P(B\mid A)\). The terminology is necessary because a
conditional probability is not a truth value assigned by the material
conditional. It stands as an assertability/uncertainty measure, differs from a
truth-functional connective, and is used to explain why high
\(P(\neg A\vee B)\) caused merely by low \(P(A)\) need not support the
indicative \cite{Adams1975}.
\index{indicative conditional}\index{conditional probability}

existing_common_goal_anchors.label: thm:p08-lewis-triviality
existing_common_goal_anchors.title: A probability-of-conditionals triviality boundary
existing_common_goal_anchors.declaration_text:
Let \(\mathcal B\) be the finite Boolean algebra generated by logically
independent events \(A,B\), so its four \(A,B\)-atoms are nonempty.  There is no
fixed event \(C\in\mathcal B\) such that
\[
 P(C)=P(B\mid A)
\]
for every strictly positive probability \(P\) on \(\mathcal B\).
Finiteness (or an explicit measure-rich extension hypothesis), the fixed-event
assumption, and membership in the same algebra are essential.  This is the
finite four-atom consequence of Lewis's source-carried triviality result; no
claim about a proof internal to this handbook is made.

existing_common_goal_anchors.label: def:p08-conditional-boundary
existing_common_goal_anchors.title: One glyph does not determine one conditional
existing_common_goal_anchors.declaration_text:
Material implication, strict implication, Stalnaker selection,
Lewis spheres, dyadic obligation, and conditional probability have different
truth or assertability clauses. A theorem transfers between them only through
an explicit translation with proved preservation; ordinary-language ``if''
does not provide that proof.

independent events \(A,B\), so its four \(A,B\)-atoms are nonempty.  There is no
fixed event \(C\in\mathcal B\) such that
\[
 P(C)=P(B\mid A)
\]
for every strictly positive probability \(P\) on \(\mathcal B\).
Finiteness (or an explicit measure-rich extension hypothesis), the fixed-event
assumption, and membership in the same algebra are essential.  This is the
finite four-atom consequence of Lewis's source-carried triviality result; no
claim about a proof internal to this handbook is made.

current_declaration_bindings.title: One glyph does not determine one conditional
current_declaration_bindings.declaration_text:
Material implication, strict implication, Stalnaker selection,
Lewis spheres, dyadic obligation, and conditional probability have different
truth or assertability clauses. A theorem transfers between them only through
an explicit translation with proved preservation; ordinary-language ``if''
does not provide that proof.

existing_common_goal_anchors.label: def:p08-adams-conditional
existing_common_goal_anchors.title: Probabilistic assertability of an indicative
existing_common_goal_anchors.declaration_text:
For events with \(P(A)>0\), the Adams-style assertability of ``if \(A\), then
\(B\)'' is governed by \(P(B\mid A)\). The terminology is necessary because a
conditional probability is not a truth value assigned by the material
conditional. It stands as an assertability/uncertainty measure, differs from a
truth-functional connective, and is used to explain why high
\(P(\neg A\vee B)\) caused merely by low \(P(A)\) need not support the
indicative \cite{Adams1975}.
\index{indicative conditional}\index{conditional probability}

current_declaration_bindings.label: def:p08-adams-conditional
current_declaration_bindings.title: Probabilistic assertability of an indicative
current_declaration_bindings.declaration_text:
For events with \(P(A)>0\), the Adams-style assertability of ``if \(A\), then
\(B\)'' is governed by \(P(B\mid A)\). The terminology is necessary because a
conditional probability is not a truth value assigned by the material
conditional. It stands as an assertability/uncertainty measure, differs from a
truth-functional connective, and is used to explain why high
\(P(\neg A\vee B)\) caused merely by low \(P(A)\) need not support the
indicative \cite{Adams1975}.
\index{indicative conditional}\index{conditional probability}

current_declaration_bindings.label: thm:p08-lewis-triviality
current_declaration_bindings.title: A probability-of-conditionals triviality boundary
current_declaration_bindings.declaration_text:
Let \(\mathcal B\) be the finite Boolean algebra generated by logically
independent events \(A,B\), so its four \(A,B\)-atoms are nonempty.  There is no
fixed event \(C\in\mathcal B\) such that
\[
 P(C)=P(B\mid A)
\]
for every strictly positive probability \(P\) on \(\mathcal B\).
Finiteness (or an explicit measure-rich extension hypothesis), the fixed-event
assumption, and membership in the same algebra are essential.  This is the
finite four-atom consequence of Lewis's source-carried triviality result; no
claim about a proof internal to this handbook is made.

current_declaration_bindings.label: def:p08-conditional-boundary
current_declaration_bindings.title: One glyph does not determine one conditional
current_declaration_bindings.declaration_text:
Material implication, strict implication, Stalnaker selection,
Lewis spheres, dyadic obligation, and conditional probability have different
truth or assertability clauses. A theorem transfers between them only through
an explicit translation with proved preservation; ordinary-language ``if''
does not provide that proof.

existing_common_goal_anchors.label: def:p08-ck-semantics
existing_common_goal_anchors.title: CK selection and premise semantics
existing_common_goal_anchors.declaration_text:
A \emph{CK selection model} assigns each world \(w\) a function
\(F_w:\mathcal P(W)\to\mathcal P(W)\), with no requirement that
\(F_w(X)\subseteq X\), and sets
\[
 M,w\models A>B
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 F_w([A])\subseteq[B].
\]
If \(F_w(\varnothing)=\varnothing\), every conditional with an impossible
antecedent is true at \(w\); basic CK does not impose that additional condition.
Equivalently, a \emph{premise-semantics presentation} assigns a relation
\(\mathcal N_w\subseteq\mathcal P(W)\times\mathcal P(W)\) and reads
\(A>B\) as \(([A],[B])\in\mathcal N_w\), where each fixed-antecedent section
is a principal filter: for some core \(K_w(X)\subseteq W\),
\((X,Y)\in\mathcal N_w\) exactly when \(K_w(X)\subseteq Y\).  Such a section
contains \(W\) and is closed under intersection and supersets.  The two
presentations correspond by
\[
 (X,Y)\in\mathcal N_w
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad F_w(X)\subseteq Y.
\]
The names are necessary because assigning a consequent-test set to an
antecedent proposition and relating premise/conclusion propositions are
different semantic data.  They
name model presentations for the same basic logic, not object-language
connectives.  Their nonredundancy is visible in the displayed conversion, and
the CK completeness theorem uses it \cite{Chellas1975}.  The absent inclusion
condition is load-bearing: adding \(F_w(X)\subseteq X\) validates the identity
schema \(A>A\), which belongs to stronger conditional systems rather than
basic \(\mathsf{CK}\).
\index{conditional logic!CK}\index{premise semantics!conditional logic}

current_declaration_bindings.label: def:p08-ck-semantics
current_declaration_bindings.title: CK selection and premise semantics
current_declaration_bindings.declaration_text:
A \emph{CK selection model} assigns each world \(w\) a function
\(F_w:\mathcal P(W)\to\mathcal P(W)\), with no requirement that
\(F_w(X)\subseteq X\), and sets
\[
 M,w\models A>B
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad
 F_w([A])\subseteq[B].
\]
If \(F_w(\varnothing)=\varnothing\), every conditional with an impossible
antecedent is true at \(w\); basic CK does not impose that additional condition.
Equivalently, a \emph{premise-semantics presentation} assigns a relation
\(\mathcal N_w\subseteq\mathcal P(W)\times\mathcal P(W)\) and reads
\(A>B\) as \(([A],[B])\in\mathcal N_w\), where each fixed-antecedent section
is a principal filter: for some core \(K_w(X)\subseteq W\),
\((X,Y)\in\mathcal N_w\) exactly when \(K_w(X)\subseteq Y\).  Such a section
contains \(W\) and is closed under intersection and supersets.  The two
presentations correspond by
\[
 (X,Y)\in\mathcal N_w
 \quad\Longleftrightarrow\quad F_w(X)\subseteq Y.
\]
The names are necessary because assigning a consequent-test set to an
antecedent proposition and relating premise/conclusion propositions are
different semantic data.  They
name model presentations for the same basic logic, not object-language
connectives.  Their nonredundancy is visible in the displayed conversion, and
the CK completeness theorem uses it \cite{Chellas1975}.  The absent inclusion
condition is load-bearing: adding \(F_w(X)\subseteq X\) validates the identity
schema \(A>A\), which belongs to stronger conditional systems rather than
basic \(\mathsf{CK}\).
\index{conditional logic!CK}\index{premise semantics!conditional logic}
